title: The hypertrophy series: the most reliable way to progressively overload
summary: NH argues that adding weight to the bar is the most reliable way to progressively overload. Tempo and rest-pause are hard to track and rarely sustained. Adding only reps or only sets drifts into low-quality volume or stalls, and evolving rep ranges only keep evolving when load goes up. Chains and bands are unnecessary for bodybuilding.
claims: Progressive overload is mandatory; without it you stagnate
Progression must be consistent: fast gains for three months followed by three months of stalling causes frustration, setbacks and lost motivation
Progression in the gym fuels the motivation to keep training
The goal of progressive overload is increasing tonnage over time, done by adding weight, changing tempo, or manipulating volume and intensity
Adding weight to the bar is the simplest, most reliable and easiest to log method, and the best for hypertrophy
Pyramid sets and drop sets create junk volume; weight progression accumulates quality tonnage
Tempo is hard to track because slow negatives and rest pauses must be timed exactly; people adopt them as a fad and drop them
Rest-pause adds time to the equation and complicates rep and set manipulation
Keep working sets straight and progressed by weight; rest-pause and pyramids can only be an afterthought
Progressing only by reps (12, 13, 14, 15 at 225 lb) drifts into rep ranges that pile up low-quality tonnage and slow progression: volume without intensity
Progressing only by adding sets at a fixed load (e.g. 315 for 2) works briefly but the sets get too easy and you stall
Evolving rep ranges grow on a horizontal plane (reps and sets) that hits a wall; going past it needs the vertical plane of added weight
For bodybuilding you can go your whole life with straight weights; chains and bands are unnecessary
Use any implement that lets you add weight (dumbbells, weighted towels, dip belts), including for bodyweight training
